steps: Leo, who is testing your app, opens the /users/:id page.
They use that part of the app the normal way, which runs the flagged line (shop/auth.py, line 18).
scenario.harm: If the stored fingerprints ever leak (a backup left open, a bug somewhere else), MD5 and SHA-1 are fast and old enough that common passwords or tokens can be worked back out in minutes.
scenario.after_fix: A slow password hash (bcrypt or argon2) is used, which makes the same work take years.

steps: Maria, who is testing your app, opens the /users/:id page.
In the box that fills in `user_id` they type: ' OR '1'='1

scenario.after_fix: The value goes in as a parameter, so the database treats it as plain text to look for, and finds nothing.

findings.title: Secret-looking setting VITE_ADMIN_SECRET is sent to every visitor's browser
findings.more_info: Variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, REACT_APP_ and similar are copied into the JavaScript that browsers download. Keep secrets in server-only variables and call them from server code.

steps: Sam opens your site and looks at the files their browser downloaded (anyone can, with the browser's developer tools).
They search them for “key” and find the value of this setting, sent to every visitor.
scenario.harm: They copy the key and use it from their own computer. Whatever the key unlocks (your database, your paid AI account, your email service) now works for them, and the bill or the data is yours.
scenario.after_fix: The key lives only on the server in an environment variable, and you replace (rotate) the old one, because anyone may already have a copy.
scenario.basis: Built by Lantern from what it found: the kind of problem comes from the rule (LW-PUBLIC-SECRET); the setting has a prefix that ships it to the browser. An illustration: Lantern read your code and did not try any of this.

findings.headline: A secret setting is sent to every visitor's browser

steps: This line is in test code. Priya never gets to it: your users do not run your tests.
scenario.harm: Python skips `assert` lines when it runs in optimised mode, so this check quietly disappears and nothing stops the bad case. In test code this is normal and fine.
scenario.after_fix: A real `if` check that raises an error, which always runs.
